The problem: practice is easy, diagnosis isn't

  • Every banking recruit must pass technicals: accounting, EV, DCF, M&A, LBO, said out loud
  • About 10–14% of each Yale SOM class goes into banking, and many more recruit
  • Anas preps 15 hours a week with six free resources, yet finding weak spots took about 2 hours, and nothing flagged the real one: answers too long

What's new: "tick and tie" every number

  • Code checks the math: a calculator computes the right answer and the wrong number each of 72 misconceptions produces
  • Placement → plan → drill, re-planned after every session
  • Concise-answer coaching, tracked over time
  • Associate, VP, Director or MD; 13 coverage groups; voice

Superday AI, IB IQ and HARDO grade with an AI rubric. None says how it checks math or publishes its accuracy.

How the agents work

Code is the boss: it picks questions and makes the grade, so no answer can talk its way to "correct" (Goodhart). Six gpt-6-luna specialists read answers and call the calculator tool; the interviewer speaks; coach and planner write. The same calculators are an MCP server.

Demo: one real run

Left: a long answer with a classic mistake. The calculator names it, the interviewer nudges without giving the answer, and the length is flagged. Right: the plan computed to the interview date.

Measured from real runs. The cheapest design (one plain LLM call) costs $0.00013 per answer, but false alarms jump to 20%–47%: rejected. Cache, code-side math and caps keep a 100-member club under $148 a year, hosting included.

Safety: 14/14 attacks stopped

  • Grader lock: code grades from calculator checks
  • Input filter: injection, hidden text, fake tags, links
  • Output filter: answer leaks, invented numbers, prompt leaks (canary)
  • Budgets: one answer at a time, rate and length caps, session, daily and global token caps
  • Least privilege: no agent can browse, email or write files
  • Independent QA: 20 more attacks held; 2 real flaws found and fixed with tests
